list.listitem: A patient with flashes, floaters, or a curtain/veil over their vision should be referred urgently to an ophthalmologist. A
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RD) is the most common type and is due to a full-thickness break in the retina. B
Surgical interventions include pneumatic retinopexy, pars plana vitrectomy, and scleral buckle. B
Patients with macula involvement may have limited final visual acuity. B
Despite successful repair, proliferative vitreoretinopathy can cause redetachment and subsequent vision loss. B

background.definition: A retinal detachment is a separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE). RDs can be rhegmatogenous, tractional, or exudative (serous).

list.listitem: All rhegmatogenous RD: 17.9 per 100,000 persons.
Idiopathic rhegmatogenous RD: 12.6 per 100,000 persons.
Traumatic rhegmatogenous RD: 1.3 per 100,000 persons.
Rhegmatogenous RD: most common type, may be due to posterior vitreous detachment or trauma.
Tractional RD: caused by diabetic retinopathy, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, penetrating trauma, or retinopathy of prematurity.
Exudative RD: rare; may be due to choroidal/retinal neoplasms, inflammatory conditions, malignant hypertension, or toxemia of pregnancy.

In all forms of RD, accumulation of fluid occurs within the potential space between the neurosensory retina and the RPE, which compromises the normal physiologic forces causing retinal adherence: RPE pump, osmotic pressure of the choroid, and mechanical forces of photoreceptor matrix.
Rhegmatogenous RD: 1 or more full thickness retinal breaks allows liquefied vitreous gel to enter the subretinal space.
Tractional RD: fibroproliferative tissue contraction lifts the retina off of the RPE.
Exudative (serous): fluid accumulates beneath the retina due to diseases of the RPE and/or choroid without the presence of a retinal break or tractional forces.
The use of oral fluoroquinolones is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. NNTH = 2500, hazard ratio 4.5.
Patients with a history of high myopia or RD should be evaluated yearly or more frequently at the discretion of an ophthalmologist. C
Patients with flashing lights, floaters, or curtain/veil over vision should be referred urgently to an ophthalmologist. A
Anterior vitreous pigment and/or vitreous hemorrhage in a symptomatic patient should raise suspicion of disease. C
Careful scleral depressed examination should be performed to evaluate for subretinal fluid and to determine the location of the retinal break. C
Careful examination of the macula should be done to determine if it is attached or detached as it affects prognosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Translucent or near opaque vitreous debris is seen; retina is flat.
Retina may appear elevated without no signs of retinal break; the elevation is smooth and dome shaped.
Blood is seen in vitreous cavity; the retina appears flat on dilated examination.
Retina may have no more than 2 to 3 optic disc areas of subretinal fluid present.
Round hole is seen in retina; retina is attached.
Pigmented lines following vessels are refractile; retina is flat.
Split of inner from outer retina is seen with refractile inner retina and involvement of inferotemporal quadrant.

list.listitem: Common symptoms include flashes of light (photopsia), floaters, and a curtain/veil over vision. Any patient with these symptoms should be referred urgently to an ophthalmologist.
Risk factors include a history of eye trauma, myopia, cataract surgery, lattice degeneration, and a history of RD in the other eye.
Visual acuity may be decreased if macula is involved or vitreous hemorrhage is obscuring visual axis. Also intraocular pressure may be lower than in the fellow eye.
The vitreous may be filled with pigment granules or red blood cells, and a posterior vitreous detachment may be seen.
The retina will appear elevated and a retinal break within the retina may be seen with or without the aide of scleral depressed examination.
If the view to the retina is obscured by a corneal scar, dense cataract, or vitreous hemorrhage, then b-scan ultrasonography can be performed to evaluate for a RD.
Optical coherence tomography may help demonstrate the degree of macular involvement in a RD, particularly if there is only shallow subretinal fluid.
Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) may be useful is the diagnosis of retinal detachment.
A patient complaining of flashing lights, floaters, and/or a curtain or veil over their vision requires urgent evaluation by an ophthalmologist.
Visual acuity can help determine if the macula is detached or attached.
Intraocular pressure in the affected eye may be lower than in the fellow eye but is not diagnostic.

Dilated examination includes noting the presence of vitreous pigment granules and/or blood, looking at the extent of the detachment, determination of the macula's involvement, and identifying a retinal break.
Only tractional and rhegmatogenous RDs are treated surgically.
Scleral buckle and pars plana vitrectomy techniques can be used successfully in both rhegmatogenous and tractional RDs. B
Pneumatic retinopexy should be reserved for simple rhegmatogenous RD due to a retinal break above the horizontal meridian in a cooperative patient. C
Surgical intervention is recommended for rhegmatogenous or tractional RDs only. Exudative detachments require treatment of the underlying disease in order to bring about resolution.

Pneumatic retinopexy is used in rhegmatogenous RD in which the retinal break is above the horizontal meridian. A gas bubble is injected intravitreously into the eye, and the patients position their head to maximally place the bubble over the retinal break. Retinal cryopexy or laser photocoagulation is then placed.

In phakic patients, scleral buckling results in statistically significant better postoperative visual acuity at 1 year with less progression of cataractous lens changes. In pseudophakic patients, pars plana vitrectomy results in greater primary anatomical success and in fewer additional procedures.

Pars plana vitrectomy is used in both tractional and rhegmatogenous RD. The subretinal fluid is drained, and tractional elements are removed with intraocular forceps. Laser or cryoretinopexy is then performed on all retinal breaks.
Pars plana vitrectomy is effective for tractional retinal detachment in people with diabetes.

Scleral buckle can be used primarily on rhegmatogenous RD and adjunctively on tractional RD. A silicone band and/or tire is wrapped around the sclera running beneath the extraocular muscles and positioned to support the retinal break and the vitreous base.
There is no evidence to support prophylactic surgical treatment of the fellow eye in a patient with unilateral giant retinal tears.
There is insufficient evidence to support surgical repair of retinal breaks or lattice degeneration to prevent retinal detachment.
Patients complaining of flashes, floaters, or curtain/veil over their vision should be referred promptly to an ophthalmologist or vitreoretinal specialist for urgent evaluation.
If left untreated, RD can lead to blindness due to macular involvement, neovascular glaucoma, cyclitic membrane formation, and phthisis bulbi. B
The macula status is critical to overall prognosis. Macula-on RD fair better visually. B
Despite successful repair, 5% to 10% of patients develop proliferative vitreoretinopathy, which may reduce visual acuity and further damage the retina. B
One percent of patients who develop severe hypertension, proteinuria, and edema in the third trimester develop exudative RD.
This usually occurs just before or immediately following delivery; the exact cause is unknown.
RD in children can be due to congenital ocular abnormalities, trauma, previous ophthalmologic surgery, or preceding uveitis.

Retinopathy of prematurity can lead to the development of RD. Babies born less than 31 weeks' gestational age and/or weighing less than 1500 g are at risk for developing ROP and are routinely screened.
ROP progresses in stages that can be treated if monitored closely using laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy.
RD can occur despite treatment or if left untreated; treatment requiring surgical intervention utilizes pars plana vitrectomy techniques and/or scleral buckle techniques.
